Write an opinion piece of about 800 words on whether cities should remove minimum parking requirements from their planning rules. Take a side and argue for it.

Do not use em dashes.

text:
**Scrap the Parking Mandate**

Every city that requires a minimum number of parking spaces for new buildings is running an experiment on its own residents. The experiment has been going for decades, the results are in, and they are not good. Cities should remove minimum parking requirements from their planning rules entirely.

Start with what these rules actually do. A minimum parking requirement tells a developer how many spaces they must build, usually as a ratio tied to apartments, square footage, or seats in a restaurant. The numbers rarely come from careful study of local demand. Many trace back to a handbook of parking generation rates compiled from a small number of suburban sites, often with ample free parking and no transit nearby. Planners copied those figures into zoning codes and they hardened into law.

The first cost is housing. A structured parking space costs tens of thousands of dollars to build, and an underground space can cost far more. That cost does not vanish. It is added to the price of every unit, whether or not the tenant owns a car. A household without a vehicle ends up subsidizing storage for other people's vehicles. In expensive cities, where every dollar of construction cost matters to whether a project pencils out, mandates can turn a feasible apartment building into an unbuilt one. Parking rules also eat land. A lot that could hold twenty homes holds fifteen and a ramp.

The second cost is urban form. When every building must surround itself with asphalt, destinations spread apart. Walking becomes unpleasant and then impractical, which makes driving more necessary, which seems to justify more parking. The mandate manufactures the demand it claims to serve. Main streets full of shops, which historically sat shoulder to shoulder, become islands separated by lots. Small businesses suffer most, because a corner building on a tight lot may be unusable for a cafe or clinic simply because it cannot meet the ratio.

Third, the rules are a blunt tool that gets the quantity wrong in both directions. In some places they force far more spaces than anyone uses, leaving lots half empty most of the year. In others, they cannot create the right kind of parking where it is scarce, because the problem there is pricing, not supply. A mandate cannot tell the difference. A developer, a lender, and a neighbor can.

Defenders raise a reasonable worry: if buildings do not provide parking, will cars flood the surrounding streets? This deserves a direct answer. First, removing a minimum is not the same as banning parking. Developers will still build it wherever customers want it, because tenants in car-dependent neighborhoods will pay for a space and lenders will often insist on one. What changes is that the amount becomes a business decision rather than a legal guess. Second, spillover onto public streets is a pricing problem with a known fix. Streets that are free to park on will always feel crowded, because a free good gets overused. Charge sensibly for curb space, or use permits and give some of the revenue back to the neighborhood, and the scramble eases. Third, the evidence from places that have acted is encouraging. Cities that have scaled back or eliminated mandates, including Buenos Aires, Minneapolis, Edmonton, and Auckland, have seen developers build less parking where it suits the site and more homes where it does not, without the chaos critics predicted. Early results are still arriving, and honest advocates should say so, but the direction is consistent.

There is also a fairness argument that tends to get lost. Today, parking is bundled into rent and housing prices, so people who drive less pay for those who drive more. Free street parking works similarly, a public asset handed out first-come, first-served. Removing the mandate lets people choose what they pay for. A student, an older person who no longer drives, or a family trying to live with one car instead of two should not have to buy two spaces they do not want.

Environmental and fiscal arguments point the same way. Less required pavement means less runoff and less heat. Compact, walkable neighborhoods generate more tax revenue per acre than sprawling, parking-heavy ones, which matters to city budgets stretched by roads and pipes that must be maintained for decades.

None of this requires a city to be hostile to drivers. Plenty of residents will keep cars, and plenty of buildings will include garages. The point is that the decision should rest with those who build, finance, and live in the buildings, not with a ratio written decades ago for a different kind of place. Cities can still set rules that serve real public goals: accessible spaces for people with disabilities, bike parking, loading zones, and safe design. Those are targeted, defensible requirements. A blanket minimum is not.

The strongest case for repeal is simple. If a space is worth building, someone will pay for it, and the market will supply it. If nobody will pay, then the law is forcing us to spend scarce money and land on something we do not want. Cities that care about affordable housing, lively streets, and sensible budgets should stop mandating it. Repeal the minimums and let the buildings, and the neighborhoods, adapt to the people who actually live in them.
